988.t: Advice to young players: learn tunes by ear

I think the best piece of advice I’ve tried to give when I’ve done the few things that I’ve done, clinics, I say well listen, take out the book, you don’t know “Body and Soul?” Sit at home, learn “Body and Soul.” When you finish learning it, take the page, rip it out, throw it out. And at…

988.t: Scales versus chords; learning by doing; Bucky's melodies
988.s: He knew chords before soloing, thinks little about scales, recalls Zoot Sims pointing at him, and praises Bucky's melody playing.
988.q: I couldn’t tell you a thing about it. And I think the way that I learned it was when you listen to George Barnes play, he knew the chords to the songs. And when I learned, the best thing that I learned was knowing the chords to the songs first. Because my father wouldn’t let me play a solo for a…

164.t: Tatum books and improvisation as a gift
164.s: Playing simplified Tatum books as a boy; he says the ability to improvise is born, not acquired.
164.q: There weren’t too many chord symbols back in the real early days of that, I mean it was pretty much the reading, and I realized very early in life if you have the ability to improvise, which is something you’re born with, I mean that’s not something you acquire, that’s just a little thing that’s…

164.s: He tells of testing students with a C chord, argues improvising cannot be taught, and says Tatum makes him want to practice.
164.q: Yeah I would disagree with that. I spent a while teaching there, and several of the students wanted to improvise and I said let me play a C chord — boom. What do you hear? What does your mind tell you play against that C chord? And most people play C- E-G. Those are the three notes of the C chord.

986.s: He requires two tunes a week played solo, and sums up improving as five daily practice items.
986.q: Yeah well I just think this is a real ADD generation too. I mean I guess my generation was also compared to previous generations. It’s really a problem.

393.t: Theory, finding his own voice and learning a solo a day
393.s: He says modern pedagogy hasn't influenced him; he now learns a Goodman or Fountain solo each day to develop his own ideas, as Kenny Davern urged.
393.q: I guess my honest answer is I’m not sure. I just kind of play things that speak to me, and I’m not quite sure what’s going on right now as far as currently, like in jazz academia, or what current guys are playing. So I guess in that sense it really hasn’t influenced me too much. For me personally,…

791.s: How she learns tunes until the harmony is inside her, and playing melody behind students as training wheels.
791.q: Well here’s the way — I’m not entirely sure. When I study a piece of music that has important harmonic material in it, I internalize it. I think this is how a lot of jazz musicians would describe the process to you, but I play it over and over and over again, both on the horn and on the piano,…

911.t: Babysitting banter and setting up a solo improvisation
911.s: Banter about his young children, and Brown prepares to play a short solo improvisation in D minor.

730.t: Teaching scales and analysis rather than names
730.s: On the Guitar Grimoire, scale catalogues and why he makes students analyze what they play.
730.q: I have a book called The Grimoire, The Guitar Grimoire. And I didn’t know this before, but grimoire is an ancient word which means a manual, a magician’s manual. I mean you open it up and you have all these spells. That kind of stuff. And it is hundreds of diagrams, all over the neck of the guitar,…

966.t: The transcription and play-along project with Cole

890.t: Mentoring at Preservation Hall and teaching a diminished lick
890.s: He never turns away a player, tries to hand things down, and demonstrates a diminished and augmented chord lick to Rowe.
890.q: I put it this way: I have never turned no one down to play with. I always play with them. But after I play with them and everything else and if I have a problem they have other musicians that replace them. We’ve got about 70 musicians associated at the hall, so why take the worst one when they’ve…

744.t: Learning licks and listening to the great players
744.s: Self-taught by copying players, he advocates collecting and practicing licks, and urges young tenor players to listen to Webster, Jacquet, Young, Byas and Ammons.
744.q: It’s a revelation to me, but that’s not what the book is, the book is about licks. I’m self taught and when I think back over it my first experience with playing when I didn’t know how to play or what to play was listening to other players play and copying, copying what they play or trying to mimic…

576.t: Learn the tune from the sheet music, not from singers
576.s: She advises learning the original melody, not copying singers who change it, using Billie Holiday as an example of organic creativity.
576.q: Okay. The reason being, there’s many reasons for this as far as I’m concerned. Being a singer myself, I’ve made a lot of mistakes. I don’t stick to the melody, I don’t all the time, I don’t deliberately try to change it, but organically something just happens musically and the spirit takes over and…

809.t: Teaching students to play wrong notes and modes
809.s: He has students practice outside notes on So What and discusses how modes are really used.
809.q: Yeah what I do is I actually make students play wrong notes. I’ll do a tune like “So What” and I’ll just say okay, let’s figure out the notes that are going to sound bad on D minor seventh, okay? 954.s: Advice: listen more, start with Lester Young, learn it like a language, acquire a taste.
954.q: Yes. I would tell them they would have to listen more. You know they would have to listen more, and maybe start off not listening to Coltrane. Start off listening to Lester Young. 1022.s: How he tells students to develop their ear by transcribing and listening widely, from Sonny Rollins to Bach.
1022.q: Well you develop your ear. In the world we live in right now jazz is not a thing that you hear on any street corner obviously, you have to go find it. So I try to tell my students to do what I did and that’s transcribe, literally develop your ear. Having a good ear is something you’re born with as…

656.t: A clinic exercise: playing with eyes closed

656.q: “Softly in the Morning Sunrise.” I think that’s the one they picked. So they started to play the tune and I listened, now how do you want to start this, what do you want to do. And they started the tune and I listened to it and I says cool, okay, all right. Let’s do it again only this time…

349.t: Scales as the foundation of jazz chords
349.s: Mullins and Rowe agree chords are built on scales, unlike classical music's melody line.
349.q: If you’re familiar with your scales, it’s not that hard. It’s not exactly easy at first because you have, in classical music you don’t deal with the chords. It’s melody line.

658.s: Contrast between old record-slowing transcription and today's information overload; how he teaches learning solos then forgetting them.
658.q: Well I would say that there’s so much information out here right now that I think the kids are bombarded with so much information. They have so much at their fingertips that sometimes they just don’t know where to start. It used to be that you’d hear something come out, you’d immediately go to your…

524.t: Teaching students about modes, math and finding their own voice
524.s: She teaches modes and the math behind beauty, and encourages students to develop their own unique selves.
524.q: Well I try to talk about it like that. And I try to just show them how I dance around and try to figure my way into music, and then I go through technical things. Modal things. And sometimes I sit down and I show them the modes, and that if you take all the modes that come from the white keys on…

932.s: He wrote his book to simplify jazz teaching, which he found too academic, like calculus without arithmetic.
932.q: Simplify jazz, yeah. Jazz Improvisation Simplified. Yeah when I was first learning how to play I would go to certain people in the area where I was going to school, before I started school, before I started my master’s in jazz studies. And they couldn’t seem to explain it to me. That’s a lot of the…

943.t: Teaching jazz by ear: singing a Parker tune on the snare
943.s: He explains his aural teaching method, having students vocalize 'Billie's Bounce' and then translate it to drums.
943.q: Okay, well for me the defining factor is how well one listens and perceives sound. And there is a very corny adage which is very true is if you can’t say it you can’t play it. So

101.t: Woods asks why the talk is about experience, not theory

851.t: Reharmonization, linear jazz and intent over execution

944.t: Playing by ear rather than by theory, and advice to students
944.s: He hears rather than sees music, calls it a gift from God, and tells students to learn scales, chords and the instrument.
944.ch: Studio work and playing by ear
944.q: Well you know 80 percent of what I do is from my ear. So 80 percent of what say Sonny Rollins does is from his eyes. He can see things and play — well Pee Wee Ellis. Pee Wee Ellis is a great example. He sees what he can hear. I hear what I can make music from. I could hear things that he can see…

515.s: Getz taught him lyricism, concision and how to serve the leader's concept and develop a melody.
515.q: Yeah. Discipline. I also learned a good lesson about how to contribute to a group and be like a valuable group member, which was to find out what was the leader’s concept and idea. I mean, at first I wasn’t thinking about that so much, and I was so thrilled about playing with Roy and Steve that…

470.t: Building vocabulary cumulatively and the tune-phrase games

413.t: Learning solos and how to practice

7.s: Thomas says putting into practice what you know led him to write one four-note chord 96 ways, and he believes jazz can be taught.
7.q: Well, you know, we were talking a while ago about you staying in New York. The idea came to me... You see, I have had so many wonderful things happen in my life, I know it just wasn't my own thinking. And it worked! I mean, the thing about it, the things work.
